title: Access Control
description: Access control principles, administration approaches, the four access control services (identification, authentication, authorization, accountability) and session management.

nodes.title: Access Control Principles
nodes.description: Three core ideas that guide every access decision: separation of duties, need to know and least privilege.

children.title: Separation of Duties
children.description: Divide key processes into multiple parts, assigned to different people, so no one person can complete a sensitive process alone.

children.title: Need to Know
children.description:
Very similar to least privilege: give users only the access they need for their job, and nothing more. The difference is subtle.
_____ restricts a user's KNOWLEDGE: access only to the data their role requires.

children.title: Least Privilege
children.description:
Restricts a user's ACTIONS to only those their role requires.
Compare need to know, which restricts a user's knowledge (access to data).

nodes.title: Administration Approaches
nodes.description:
How access to systems is administered: adding, changing and removing users.
Three main approaches: centralized, decentralized and hybrid.

children.title: Centralized
children.description: Access to many separate applications is managed through one central system.

children.title: Decentralized
children.description: Access to each application is managed separately, within that application.

children.title: Hybrid
children.description: Some combination of centralized and decentralized. Many organizations use this approach.

nodes.title: Access Controls Services
nodes.description:
Every access control system must provide four major services: identification, authentication, authorization and accountability.
Access controls are the mechanisms that work together to protect an organization's assets. They can be physical, like locks, or logical, like a login to an operating system. They let management specify which users can access which resources, what operations they can perform, and hold each individual accountable.
Every access control system controls a subject's access to an object through mediation based on a set of rules, with everything logged and monitored. This is the Reference Monitor Concept (RMC). An implementation of the RMC is a security kernel, so every access control system is a security kernel.

children.title: Identification
children.description:
The user asserts their identity to the system.
Example: a username, such as rwitcher.

children.title: Authentication
children.description: The system verifies the user's identity using one of the three factors of authentication: knowledge, ownership or characteristic.

children.title: Knowledge
children.description: Something you know: the user proves their identity with information they have memorized.

children.title: Password
children.description: A memorized secret the user provides to authenticate.

children.title: Passphrase
children.description: A long sequence of words that is easy to remember.

children.title: Questions
children.description:
Security _____ the user answers, with answers the user set up in advance.
Example: the name of a first pet.

children.title: Ownership
children.description: Something you have: things in the user's possession.

children.title: One-time Passwords
children.description:
The most common form of authentication by ownership.
A hard or soft token generates a code that is valid for a single login only.

children.title: Hard Tokens
children.description:
Dedicated physical devices, such as a key fob with a small display, that generate one-time passwords.
Example: an RSA ID key.

children.title: Soft Tokens
children.description:
Apps on a general-purpose device that generate one-time passwords.
Example: the Microsoft or Google authenticator apps on a mobile phone.

children.title: Synchronous
children.description:
One of the two types of one-time password token, based on time.
The token and the authentication server each generate the same one-time password every 30 to 60 seconds, because their clocks are kept in step.

children.title: Asynchronous
children.description:
Uses a challenge and a response. The user receives a challenge, enters it into the token, and the token generates the response: the one-time password.
Rare, because it is more expensive and complicated, but more secure. Used in high-value situations, such as Bloomberg financial terminals.

children.title: Smart / Memory Cards
children.description:
Cards used for authentication by ownership, besides one-time password tokens. Two kinds:
- One kind contains a computer chip that can process data, so it is more secure.
- The other kind only stores data that can be read. It is the same data every time, so it is less secure.

children.title: Characteristic
children.description:
Something you are: the user proves their identity with a trait of their body or of how they behave.
Called _____, not just biometrics, because there are two kinds: physiological and behavioral.

children.title: Physiological
children.description: Traits of our bodies, such as fingerprints, hand geometry, vein patterns, face, iris and retina. Often called biometrics.

children.title: Fingerprint
children.description: Scans our fingerprints.

children.title: Hand Geometry
children.description: Measures the overall dimensions of the hand.

children.title: Vascular Pattern
children.description:
Scans vein patterns, often on the back of the hand.
Many Pearson VUE test centers use vascular scanners when you register for the CISSP exam, to make sure it is you who comes back into the room after a break, not someone hired to write the exam for you.

children.title: Facial
children.description: Measures features of the face, such as the distance between the eyes, nose and mouth, and the shape of the jawline.

children.title: Iris
children.description: Scans the colored ring of the eye: the outside of the eyeball.

children.title: Retina
children.description:
Scans the vein pattern at the back of the eye: the inside of the eyeball.
Usually considered the most accurate biometric system.

children.title: Behavioral
children.description: How we act and do things, such as speaking, typing and walking.

children.title: Voice
children.description: Analyzes the way we speak: the fine details of our voices.

children.title: Signature
children.description: Analyzes how we write our name by hand, including the shape, speed and pressure of the pen strokes.

children.title: Key Stroke
children.description: Analyzes how we type, using characteristics such as dwell time (how long a key is held down) and flight time (the time between keys).

children.title: Gait
children.description: Gait dynamics: analyzes how we walk.

children.title: Templates
children.description:
A biometric system processes a user's sample, such as a fingerprint or face scan, to find unique characteristics, and creates a mathematical representation of them: the biometric template.
Two major uses:
- 1 to N (one to many) lookup, for identification
- 1 to 1 direct comparison, for authentication

children.title: Type 1: False Reject
children.description:
Biometric authentication is not binary: the system is never 100% sure a user is valid or invalid, so it can make two types of errors.
This error: a valid user is wrongly refused access. Inconvenient, but not a breach.

children.title: Type 2: False Accept
children.description: The more dangerous biometric error: an invalid user, such as an attacker, is wrongly authenticated and given access.

children.title: Crossover Error Rate
children.description:
Type 1 and Type 2 error rates are inverse to each other: lowering one raises the other. On a graph, the two lines intersect at the _____, also called the Equal Error Rate (EER).
It is a good measure of a biometric system's overall accuracy: the lower it is, the more accurate the system.

children.title: Single / Multifactor
children.description:
How many authentication factors are combined:
- One factor alone: knowledge, ownership or characteristic, such as just a password.
- Two or more DIFFERENT factors, such as a password plus a token. A password and a PIN are both knowledge, so together they still count as one factor.

children.title: Authenticator Assurance Levels (AAL)
children.description:
A model that measures how robust and secure an authentication process is.
Three levels, defined by NIST in SP 800-63B: level 1 is the least secure and level 3 the most secure.

children.title: Just-in-time Access
children.description:
Grants a user access to a system exactly when it is needed, and only for as long as a specific task takes.
Instead of standing access, users get permissions dynamically when they need them, and the permissions are revoked once the task is done.

children.title: Authorization
children.description:
Defines a user's specific access within a system: what they are allowed to access and do.
This is where principles such as least privilege and need to know are applied.
Three access control philosophies: discretionary, non-discretionary and mandatory.

children.title: Discretionary
children.description:
The owner of the system decides who is authorized to access what.
A very good security practice: owners understand their systems best, and are accountable for their security.

children.title: Rule
children.description: Access is decided by a list of _____ in a file, or an ACL (access control list). A request that matches an entry is allowed or denied.

children.title: Role
children.description: Create _____, define the access for each _____, usually by job function, then assign one or more _____ to a user. A user's _____ define their access.

children.title: Types of RBAC
children.description:
Four major types to be familiar with:
- Non-RBAC: no role-based access.
- Limited RBAC: roles are created within specific applications, and a role defines access only in that application.
- Hybrid RBAC: one role can define a user's access in several applications, but not every application in the organization is integrated.
- Full RBAC: one role can grant access to any application across the organization.
Most companies do not reach full RBAC. They use limited or hybrid RBAC.

children.title: Attribute / Context
children.description:
Decides access from properties of the user, the asset and the situation of each request, not from a fixed list or a job function.
Examples: source IP address, geolocation, OS type, classification of the asset being accessed, and so on.

children.title: Non-discretionary
children.description:
Someone other than the owner decides who is authorized to access what, such as an IT help desk person.
Not a good security practice.

children.title: Mandatory
children.description:
The system decides, based on the security clearance of users and the classification of assets.
Labeling is an important requirement for mandatory access.

children.title: Accountability
children.description:
The final and most important access control service.
To have security, users must be accountable for their actions on a system.

children.title: Principle of Access Control
children.description:
Accountability is the most important access control service, so it has a special name: the _____.
The _____ and accountability mean the same thing.

nodes.title: Session Management
nodes.description:
A session begins once a user has been identified, authenticated and authorized into a system.
Session management keeps these sessions secure.

children.title: Session Hijacking
children.description: The major risk related to sessions: an attacker takes over a valid user's session, for example by stealing the session ID, and acts as that user.
